name: GNU Hurd
summary: Set of servers and daemons running on the GNU Mach microkernel, forming the official kernel of the free GNU operating system designed by the Free Software Foundation.
license: Open Source (GNU General Public License v2 or later)

content.introduction: GNU Hurd is the official kernel developed by the GNU project, initiated in 1983 by Richard Stallman and the Free Software Foundation (FSF) with the aim of offering an entirely free Unix-compatible operating system. Although the majority of GNU systems today use the Linux monolithic kernel (forming the GNU/Linux system), Hurd development began as early as 1990 to realise the original FSF vision: a modular microkernel system, extensible, resilient and granting every user extensive control over their system services without requiring administrator privileges.
content.origin_and_history:
The GNU project was launched in 1983 by Richard Stallman in order to produce a complete and free operating system. The February 1986 GNU bulletin designates TRIX, developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as the intended kernel; in December 1986, the Free Software Foundation states that it has begun the necessary modifications to TRIX, then starts in spring 1987 negotiations with Professor Rashid, of Carnegie-Mellon University, about the Mach kernel. The project places the start of Hurd development in 1990, and the November 1991 bulletin presents the Hurd running on Mach as the official GNU kernel.

The chronology published by the project, which presents it as incomplete, then lists GNU Hurd 0.1 on 6 September 1996, GNU Mach 1.0 on 14 April 1997, GNU 0.2 on 16 June 1997, GNU Mach 1.2 on 21 June 1999, GNU Mach 1.3 on 27 May 2002, then the joint releases Hurd 0.5, Mach 1.4 and MIG 1.4 on 27 September 2013, Hurd 0.6 on 10 April 2015, 0.7 on 31 October 2015, 0.8 on 18 May 2016 and 0.9 on 18 December 2016. The project home page states that there is no stable version, that the sources are mainly distributed through Git and that the latest release is GNU Hurd 0.9.
content.what_is_it: Technically, GNU Hurd is not a single conventional kernel, but a suite of specialised software servers running in user space on top of the **GNU Mach** microkernel (a variant derived from Mach 3.0 developed at Carnegie Mellon University). GNU Mach handles the primitive thread scheduling operations, virtual address space management and inter-process communication (IPC) based on Mach ports. The Hurd servers implement the network protocols, file systems, authentication and POSIX signals in unprivileged space.
content.multi_server_microkernel_and_mach_ipc: The Hurd architecture rests on a clear separation of responsibilities between independent daemons. The `proc` server manages the process table and the assignment of identifiers (PIDs); the `auth` server handles identification tokens and access privileges; the `exec` server ensures the loading and execution of ELF-format binaries; the `pflocal` server manages the local sockets of the Unix domain, while `pfinet` provides the TCP/IP network stack. These components communicate by exchanging asynchronous messages through the Mach IPC channels, whose RPC interfaces are generated automatically by the MIG (Mach Interface Generator) stub compiler. A failure in an application server therefore does not cause a global crash of the machine.
content.translators_and_flexible_vfs_architectur: The most emblematic innovation of GNU Hurd lies in the concept of **translator**. A translator is a program running in user space that attaches to a node of the file system tree and dynamically controls access to it. Passive translators are stored on disk as metadata and activated on demand; active translators run in memory. Any ordinary user can attach their own translators to their personal directories through the `settrans` command without needing `root` privileges: it thus becomes possible to mount an ISO image, a compressed archive or a remote file system (FTP, HTTP) in the form of a simple transparent directory.
content.security_model_and_authentication_server:
The design document Towards a New Strategy of OS Design describes the Hurd authentication model. Each port addressed to the authentication server identifies a user and associates with it a credentials block containing sets of user and group identifiers, possibly empty. This server provides three services: boolean operations that produce, from two authentication ports, a third port representing the union of the two sets; the ability, for any user whose identifier is zero, to create an arbitrary authentication port; remote procedure calls allowing clients and servers that do not trust each other to establish their identity. A user program can implement the authentication protocol without compromising security, but a service that authenticates a user addresses the server it trusts and refuses the transaction if the user employs another one; this constraint imposes the same server on all programs, which justifies a separate password server, responsible for delivering authorisation tokens in exchange for passwords.

Translators gain no privilege from their attachment to the file system: they run with the identifier of the owner of the translated file and can only be set or modified by that owner. The document plans thirty-two-bit user and group identifiers, an author identifier specific to each file, modifiable by the owner, and an additional set of permission bits for the unknown user, distinct from the "world" category applied to known users.

The Debian GNU/Hurd configuration page adds that processes do not keep an identity fixed at their creation: they hold identity tokens separate from the process, which can be added by a competent authority or destroyed. This text describes the design of the system and not a hardening procedure, and the Debian port does not aim at the performance and stability of a production system.
content.posix_compliance_glibc_and_debian_port: To guarantee interoperability with software written for the Unix world, GNU Hurd relies on a complete implementation of the POSIX interface provided by the project standard C library, **glibc** (GNU C Library). The vast majority of GNU utilities, compilation tools (GCC, Make, Binutils) and development environments work identically under Hurd. The most stable and accessible incarnation of the system is the **Debian GNU/Hurd** distribution, maintained by the Debian project in the form of an official port without the Linux kernel. About three quarters of the packages of the Debian archive are ported to it, according to the porting page.
content.installation_of_debian_gnu_hurd:
The GNU project does not recommend bootstrapping Hurd from source by cross-compilation and refers to a binary distribution; Debian provides this port under the name Debian GNU/Hurd, published in the unstable branch of the Debian archive and presented as a development, server and desktop platform.

Installation is done with the Debian installer. The images of the hurd-i386 port are published in `cdimage.debian.org/cdimage/ports/stable/hurd-i386/`, those of the hurd-amd64 port, still in preview, in `cdimage.debian.org/cdimage/ports/latest/hurd-amd64/`. The Debian project reports two constraints specific to the port: swap must be enabled, failing which Mach encounters difficulties when memory is saturated, and no separate partition must be mounted on `/usr`, on pain of boot failure. If Hurd occupies the machine alone, the installer can install GRUB itself.

A preinstalled `debian-hurd.img.tar.gz` image is also published and can be started with `kvm -m 2G`; the page recommends the KVM virtual machine as the simplest and best-tested method, physical hardware support varying between machines.
content.hardware_support_maturity_and_limitation: The reference hardware platform of GNU Hurd is the **32-bit x86 (i386)** architecture. Recent major work has made it possible to boot and consolidate a port to the **x86-64 (AMD64)** architecture with a working 64-bit user space. Although it is a historical project active for more than thirty years, Hurd remains classified as an experimental system. Its practical limitations include the absence of native support for wireless technologies (Wi-Fi), partial USB support relying on virtualised drivers (DDE/Rump layer), and symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) support still being stabilised in GNU Mach. The system is particularly suited to virtual machines (QEMU, KVM, VirtualBox) and to x86 test machines.
advantages: Official kernel of the GNU project illustrating a modular and elegant microkernel architecture.
Revolutionary translator mechanism allowing ordinary users to extend the file system without root rights.
Isolation of system services in user space limiting the impact of failures or security flaws.
Excellent POSIX compatibility thanks to the close integration with the GNU C Library (glibc).
Debian GNU/Hurd software ecosystem giving access to thousands of proven open-source packages.
Project under the free GNU GPL licence guaranteeing the durability and freedom of use of the code.
disadvantages: Development stage still experimental after more than three decades of work.
I/O and IPC communication performance lower than modern highly optimised monolithic kernels.
Incomplete hardware support on recent physical machines (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, fine-grained power management).
Multicore (SMP) support still incomplete at the GNU Mach level.
Unsuited to critical production servers or daily professional workstations.
who_is_it_for: Computer science researchers, teachers and students exploring microkernel architectures and distributed systems.
Fervent free software advocates wishing to run the original GNU system as designed by the FSF.
Developers curious to experiment with user-space server programming and VFS translators.
Debian users interested in non-Linux architectures in a virtualised environment.
who_is_it_not_for: Users looking for a stable operating system for daily office or multimedia use.
Enterprises looking for a hosting server solution with industrial performance guarantees and commercial support.
Owners of recent modern computer hardware requiring Wi-Fi or 3D graphics acceleration drivers.
Deployment infrastructures for native Linux containers (Docker, Kubernetes).
content.verdict: GNU Hurd is an experimental project of the GNU project. By rethinking the structure of operating systems through a constellation of cooperating servers and its translator mechanism, it implements a microkernel architecture. Although it remains experimental compared with Linux, it retains educational and historical interest.

components.name: GNU Mach
components.note: Microkernel on which the Hurd servers run, according to the project page; the page cites patches that landed in GNU Mach.

components.name: Hurd servers
components.note: Collection of servers implementing file systems, network protocols and file access control on top of Mach.

components.name: Hurd translators
components.note: User-space translators implementing file systems and other services; the project page cites, among others, an experimental 9P translator.

relations.name: Debian
relations.note: Major Linux distribution providing the most complete official port of the GNU user space with the Hurd kernel (Debian GNU/Hurd).

relations.name: FreeBSD
relations.note: Free Unix operating system with a monolithic kernel representing the traditional approach compared with the microkernel architecture of Hurd.

relations.name: Redox OS
relations.note: Modern free operating system founded on a microkernel architecture.

relations.name: Linux From Scratch
relations.note: Project documenting the step-by-step construction of the GNU operating system with an independent kernel.
